barrow.json.text:
A barrow is a pre-Celtic grave. Builders set stones in a line that ends in a burial mound. Some barrows hold more than one body.

The Wiltshire Downs carry the largest group of barrows in England. Stonehenge rises above those downs. Barrows also appear throughout Ireland. Local people revere the graves near their homes. They tell tales of hauntings at the mounds. Black Dogs of the fairy race and wandering ghosts frequent these sites. See the entry for the Fairy Mound.

bean_nighe.json.text:
The bean nighe is an Irish and Scottish folk figure. She is the Washer at the Ford. She acts as a form of the banshee. This death prophet arrives before a death.

She washes the clothes of the doomed in a river or a stream. A passerby hears a noise like rippling water. That noise is her slapping the wet clothes. She appears as a small woman in a green gown. Her feet are red and webbed.

Some say she is the ghost of a woman who died in childbirth. That mother left her laundry unfinished. Others count her among the fairy race. She can see things in the future beyond the death. If you catch sight of her before she sees you, you may request a prophecy. Her prophecy always proves accurate. The chance to ask still brings risk.

bean_tighe.json.text:
The bean tighe is the Fairy Housekeeper of Irish folktale. She lives at the bottom of the enchanted Lough Gur. This lake sits in County Limerick.

Once every seven years the lake water drains away. The dry lake bed then reveals her. The fairy housekeeper walks across the exposed floor. She reaches a stone chair on the shore. She sits there for a few hours. When the water returns, she disappears once more.

key_results: The fairy housekeeper dwells at the bottom of Lough Gur.

bear.json.text:
The bear is a symbolic animal. It sees dimly but hears with sharp ears. The creature runs fast and climbs with skill. Early people gave the bear their fear and their respect. They prized the strength of the beast.

The bear can stand and walk like a man. A skinned bear looks like the carcass of a person. These habits made people think of the bear as nearly human.

The Celts had their origin in the mountains of central Europe. That land was prime bear country. Caves in the Alps hold signs of an old bear cult. That worship may have shaped the Celtic view of the bear. The name Berne means the bear. A sculpture there shows Artio, the Celtic bear goddess.

key_results: The bear was feared and respected for its strength and speed.

beating_the_bounds.json.text:
Beating the bounds is a British rural ritual. Folk in the English countryside walk the lines of their parish on set holidays. They kept this custom until recent times. A priest or a minister leads the walk. The rite likely reaches back to pre-Christian days.

When the walk passes ancient Standing Stones, the guide presses children against the boulders. The children also get ducked in a sacred spring or a pond along the route. In this way the young learn the limits of their parish.

key_results: Folk in rural England walked the lines of their parish on set holidays.

bee.json.text:
Bees rarely appear in Celtic legend. When they do come, they stand for wisdom. The bee was said to be a drop that fell from heaven.

On the Isle of Man, fishermen caught bees in the early spring. Each sailor carried a bee as an amulet of safety at sea. In Ireland the bee had no pre-Christian mark of religion. Some Irish saints still kept bees. The Welsh saint Domnoc and the Munster nun Gobnat were tied to the craft of keeping bees.

key_results: Bees appear as a symbol of wisdom in rare Celtic tales.

beech_tree.json.text:
The beech is one of the sacred trees of the Celts. This tree belongs to the genus Fagus. It stands as a large close kin of the oak. Its gray trunk looks thick and muscular. Its crown hangs low and full.

The beech held an honored place among the sacred plants of the Celts. Its wide branches cast a broad shade. Many a grove gave the tree its glory. The shape stayed low and full for the life of the tree.

bilberry.json.text:
The bilberry is a symbolic plant of Ireland. Its Latin name is Vaccinium myrtillus. The fruit is also called the whortleberry or the mulberry. It has been a calendar marker of Ireland up to today.

Folk climb the hills at Lughnasa to gather the berries. They eat the fruit on the spot or save it for pies and wine. They say the berries lose their flavor after Lughnasa. The start of the berry season also opens the harvest.

People read omens from the berry bushes at this time. Plenty of berries meant a good crop would come. A few berries warned that hunger and hard times drew near.

bile__bele__pl___bili_.json.text:
A bile is a sacred tree. It often grows beside a holy well or another honored place. People in Ireland still hang strips of cloth on the branches. These cloth strips are called clooties. The tree droops with these offerings today.

In old times a bile marked the place where a king was installed. Its branches were cut to shape the ruler's staff. A god named Bile also appears in Irish legend. He is the ancestral father of the Milesians. They were the last invaders of Ireland.

It may be that the tree holds a link to the god. The link is not certain. The term bile names a sacred tree of any species. Oak, yew, and ash held the chief power. The Dindsenchas, the place poems, sing of the great trees of Ireland. They tell of an oak that bore nuts and apples along with its acorns. The Yew of Ross was a firm strong god. The Ash of Uisneach fell and spread out fifty miles.

key_results: A bile marks a sacred tree beside a holy well.

birch_tree.json.text:
The birch is one of the sacred plants of the Celts. Its sign holds the second slot of the Tree Alphabet. The birch species betula is short-lived. Still it is graceful, with pale white bark.

The wood of the birch gives a pole to hold. The Celts shaped it into a Maypole for the dances. Those dances came at the feast of Beltane. So the birch holds its place in the rites of the old Celts.
